8514.d:
An exploration of algorithmic organisms in a contained environment.

This piece is about the simulation of microscopic patterns using a high number of even tinier agents all following the same rules. Different species evolve and interact together, resulting in stabilizing patterns out of their parametric configurations. A form of artificial life.

This work is based on the paper "Characteristics of pattern formation and evolution in approximations of physarum transport networks", written by Jeff Jones and popularized in the artistic field by Sage Jenson. Some features were added to increase the visual and behavioral complexity of the system. Agents are divided into different species, with their own set of rules and interacting with their own substrate. Substrates also interact with each other and agents will mutate in contact of some of them.

8523.d:
p32 honey farm hassler is a period-32 oscillator, sparker, and honey farm hassler that was originally discovered by David Raucci and praosylen on September 9, 2021. In terms of its 45 cells, it is currently the smallest known period-32 oscillator.

It was first found in a dimerized form containing two copies of Richs p16. praosylen found that it could be monomerized with only one honey farm predecessor and with one of the p16s replaced with a figure eight, producing a 64-cell oscillator that was already smaller than gourmet, the previous record holder. Raucci then found that the other p16 could also be replaced with a figure eight, giving a 48-cell form. A 14-glider synthesis of this oscillator was found the day of its discovery. On January 4, 2022, iNoMed found that the figure eight could be replaced by a mold, giving a p32 oscillator with only 45 cells.

wwei23 discovered that the spark from the monomer form could convert a blinker into a glider.

8549.d:
Edouard Manet  was a French modernist painter. He was one of the first 19th-century artists to paint modern life, as well as a pivotal figure in the transition from Realism to Impressionism.

His early masterworks, The Luncheon on the Grass and Olympia, both 1863, caused great controversy and served as rallying points for the young painters who would create Impressionism. Today, these are considered watershed paintings that mark the start of modern art.

Although harshly condemned by critics who decried its lack of conventional finish, Manets work had admirers from the beginning. One was Emile Zola, who wrote in 1867: "We are not accustomed to seeing such simple and direct translations of reality. Then, as I said, there is such a surprisingly elegant awkwardness ... it is a truly charming experience to contemplate this luminous and serious painting which interprets nature with a gentle brutality."

8564.d:
Solace is an algorithm that generates artworks of sand dunes. It draws hundreds of thousands of tiny points according to a probability distribution calculated from the positions of the dunes.

The logic to divide the dunes into light and dark sides is simple, but produces some interesting chaotic behaviour. These are details that weren't hard-coded but emerge organically, such as the patterns on the spines of the dunes or the stripes around their bases.

Please note that the algorithm can take some time to run, especially when the number of dunes is high.

The starting price at unlock will be 12 tez. After 5 minutes, it will be reduced to 6 tez and after another 5 minutes, it will be reduced to the resting price of 3 tez.

Created by lunarean.

8578.d:
Imagined coral-like creatures grown in a generative lab, released into the wild on fxhash.

Every variation is a unique generative curation of algorithmic choices. The resultant forms are at once both delicate and muscular.  Are they alive? Could they survive in the wild? 

The algorithm creates the skeleton of each creature from a set of anchor points and uses quadratic interpolation between the points to create the core shape. A rotating brush consisting of layered polygons of varying structures and patterns then follows the shape, twisting and turning and it goes. Generative features assigned to the brush then determines the resultant shape.

W to toggle wide mode

68P16 (or p16 wing hassler) is a period-16 oscillator discovered by carybe in a symmetric soup on October 22, 2018 using apgsearch.[1] It consists of eight blocks hassling four wings and four blocks, and produces useful sparks.

A 42-glider synthesis for this oscillator was found by Mark Niemiec on November 2, 2018, which was improved to 39 by 2718281828 later that day.

On September 15, 2021, David Raucci used this oscillator to construct a period-32 glider gun, smaller than the original p32 glider gun using a completely different mechanism that was posted just a few days earlier.

8601.d:
When I was a youngster, my favorite arcade game was Tempest. When I was an oldster, with more money than sense, I saw an original Tempest machine on Craigslist, and bought it. Now I can play Tempest whenever I want. 

This by way of saying that I love vector graphics. I love how, when the electron guns are out of alignment, any time the machine tries to make the color white, fast-moving objects become red, green, and blue lines. I love the trails that movement leaves on the CRT. I love the flicker. 

I tried to reproduce all those effects in this mint. There is a special red mode that has nothing to do with Tempest, but I thought it looked cool and would be a fun rarity. 

Created in p5.js

8616.d:
Gustave Caillebotte was a French painter who was a member and patron of the Impressionists, although he painted in a more realistic manner than many others in the group. Caillebotte was noted for his early interest in photography as an art form.

In common with his precursors Jean-François Millet and Gustave Courbet, as well his contemporary Degas, Caillebotte aimed to paint reality as it existed and as he saw it, hoping to reduce the inherent theatricality of painting. Perhaps because of his close relationship with so many of his peers, his style and technique vary considerably among his works, as if "borrowing" and experimenting, but not really sticking to any one style. At times, he seems very much in the Degas camp of rich-colored realism (especially his interior scenes); at other times, he shares the Impressionist commitment to "optical truth" and employs an impressionistic pastel-softness and loose brush strokes most similar to Renoir and Pissarro, although with a less vibrant palette.

8636.d:
Charge is a bridge between engineering and art. It marks beginnings as it is the first long-form algorithm I started developing after joining the NFT and crypto scene. 

The algorithm uncovers the interaction between charged particles in a vacuum, dropping particles in the resulting electromagnetic field showing us a unique view into a subatomic vastness. 

Visually, Charge utilises procedural colour palettes to make each and every piece unique. The layout of the charged particles is another feature that has a large impact on the resulting field and is finely tuned to give a high chance of showcasing a wide range of variations of interacting charges.

Depending on the device, the setup of the simulation may take up to a minute to load.

Original artwork by TENGIL in Stockholm, February 2022.

Under the hood Charge makes use of the MIT-licensed libraries p5js and poisson-disk-sampling.

8649.d:
What is a movement and its trajectory? The shortest path is a straight line. If I fly straight from Taiwan to Iceland and continue my journey straight, will l end up in Taiwan again?

"Pulsar rotation" reflects the fundamentals of motion in the universe. The movement may be chaotic on some local segment, but it always obeys the main rule - the movement is always forward. We cannot see the scale of the infinite forward motion, but we can estimate it by recreating a model of infinity visible for us entirely. And here generative art comes to our aid - to show what we can only imagine in theory.

"Pulsar rotation” is an endless dance of noise particles. Sometimes with a fading effect and a subsequent recovery. The particle leaves a colour trail after itself, which adds an additional colour shade to the bouquet.

Each edition is assigned 1 out of 197 countries. Four basic LGBT+ rights are represented as circles with barriers. One barrier means full rights. The more barriers, the more unequal rights are afforded to LGBT+ people.

Once fully minted, I recommend using the fxhash filters to look deeper into the data set.

More background on my Twitter: @ada_ada_ada_art

Mobile - Long press / Double tap

8666.c:
Barriers is an artwork+data visualization about the state of LGBT+ rights across the world.

Each edition is assigned 1 out of 197 countries. Four basic LGBT+ rights are represented as circles with barriers. The largest circle signifies whether homosexual activity is legal. The second-largest signifies same-sex marriage. The third one, same-sex adoption. The smallest one is the legality of gender change. One barrier means full rights. The more barriers, the more unequal rights are afforded to LGBT+ people.

The colors of the edition signify the country’s region and subregion.

The artwork adapts to different screen sizes and ratios, so I recommend exploring it on various devices or resizing your browser window.

8670.d:
This work lies at the intersection of 3 stories from first half of XX century

1. 1924: De Stijl is famous for its colors and patterns, Mondrian is the best known painter in this movement, but also he was friends with Theo Van Doesburg. However, the story goes that they had some disagreements, exact reason is unknown, but the legend is that Mondrian never accepted diagonals, while Theo insisted on their dynamic aspects.
2. 1908: Voronoi studies the famous partition of n-dimensional spaces, now bearing his name by "Voronoi diagrams".
3. 1915: Start of suprematism with Malevich's Black Square. This generative piece employs the craquelure from this painting, which also sometimes is used as a symbol of authenticity : )

The work is done with p5.js and p5.voronoi libraries.
Usually it has the palette of Piet Mondrian, with jagged edges (as some kind of middle ground between him and Theo); but rare cases include straight lines, and also color palettes from several of Van Doesburg artworks.

8697.d:
A "Cellular Skyscraper" originates from a 15x15 grid with 15x3 cells randomly assigned the 'alive' state. According to the cellular automaton rule chosen from the transaction hash 24 new generations are calculated and placed on top of each other.

There are four different rules available (listed in Golly notation) all based on the Moore neighbourhood: 

B3/S23 (Game of Life)
B36/S125 (2x2)
B368/S245 (Morley)
B3/S234 (didn't find a name for it but produces interesting large structures)

After all generations have been calculated the algorithm searches through the complete 3D grid to find the one structure consisting of the most connected alive cells - cells are connected when they have at least one alive neighbour in any of the three axis.

Features are cell count, height, highlight color, ca rule and antenna count.

Extra: press 'd' to download the structure as a .gltf file to import into Blender or other software.

Swimbots are colorful wiggly creatures that evolved out of my artificial life experiments beginning in the mid 1990's. Now, as the result of a creative collaboration with Canton Becker, we're offering a limited number of artfully-mutated swimbots and releasing them into the wild, as NFTs.

Each NFT is a portrait of a unique swimbot flaunting its characteristic shape, wiggle, and coloration against a stylized background. Some backgrounds are quite rare.

Swimbots NFTs are more interesting when they interact! When placed into a common "gene pool", they mate, compete for food, and evolve... essentially forever. To that end, every NFT will also be spawned in a pool on the swimbots website. NFT holders can use this site to run simulations and competitions to see how good their swimbots are at propagating their genes into the future. Will your swimbot sink or swim?

https://www.swimbots.com/nft

8706.d:
The imagery used in this work began as an original photograph by the artists. During post-production, a single row of pixels was selected in each photograph and then stretched outwards in both directions to fill the entire frame. These rigid 'stretched pixel' compositions were then further manipulated into various painterly ‘pixel forms’. The works in the ‘Painterly Pixels’ series are generated by drawing upon 199 unique 'pixel forms'.

The 199 unique 'pixel forms' have been organised across 19 separate layers. When a work is generated, it will take one 'pixel form' from each layer. There is an equal probability for every ‘pixel form’, across each of the 19 layers. The number of 'pixel form' variations available at each layer are as follows: 21, 11, 8, 9, 11, 12, 9, 11, 10, 10, 12, 11, 11, 8, 12, 8, 5, 6, 14. 

Each work is 1000 x 1000 pixels - please enjoy every single one of them.

8719.d:
'What on Earth?' expands upon the history of my last piece 'Terra'. This is a speculative scifi projection taking inspiration from the IPCC reports on climate change. This piece is an imagination of the possibility of the multiverse. 

It is a generative art piece that uses six base maps for the different types of earth. The two other layers are procedurally generated and overlayed on each other resulting in 6x4x5 possible combinations. However there is always a chance of getting multiple planetary accessories which increase the number of unique possible variations. Each of the pieces also come with their unique version of narrative embedded in the piece itself. 

Instruction:
Hover in the top right corner of the canvas to reveal a button to access the story and the settings. This is an interactive piece - click and drag to turn/play with your earth. 

Photosensitivity Warning: Viewer discretion is advised before you turn on 'Acid' inside settings. It involves flashing imagery and glitching effects.
